author: Philip K. Dick

page_summary:
An overcrowded, dystopian Earth is offered apparent salvation by Trails of Hoffman Limited, a corporation that instantaneously teleports emigrants to a colony world, Whale's Mouth, advertised as an idyllic new home. The catch: no return trip exists, and no independent verification of conditions on Whale's Mouth has ever reached Earth, since only teleportation -- never conventional travel -- connects the two worlds. Rachmael ben Applebaum, whose family's slower-than-light passenger ship business has been driven to ruin by the teleportation monopoly, undertakes an eighteen-year non-teleported voyage specifically so that at least one human being will reach the colony by conventional means and be able to independently verify what is actually there -- and, if the propaganda is false, be able to report it back before any additional emigrants are lied into a one-way trip to disaster. The novel intercuts Rachmael's voyage with escalating corporate and governmental intrigue back on Earth as Trails of Hoffman's leadership works to suppress the possibility that its advertised paradise might be exposed as something far worse, revealed by novel's end to be a captured territory under hostile alien control, with the emigration program a mechanism for supplying alien conquerors with a docile human population.

**Why it matters.** Lies, Inc. is Dick's own 1984 expansion of his 1966 novel The Unteleported Man, and the two versions are frequently studied together as a case study in Dick's revision practices late in his career. The novel's central device -- a one-way, unverifiable teleportation link exploited to conceal a hostile reality from an eager, credulous population -- is one of Dick's most direct science-fictional metaphors for propaganda and corporate-state collusion, anticipating later fiction and film about advertised utopias concealing genuine danger. Rachmael's decision to take the slow, verifiable path specifically to preserve the possibility of independent truth-telling gives the novel an unusually explicit epistemological argument: that some truths are worth the enormous cost of confirming firsthand rather than trusting to convenience.

*The revelation that Whale's Mouth serves a hostile alien occupation recasts the entire emigration program not as a well-intentioned failure but as an active, ongoing betrayal -- one Rachmael's decade-plus voyage was undertaken specifically to expose.*
